scope: 对两个无解释样板的知识地图节点完成外部课程标准、专业框架和教学研究依据核查；本批不创建解释样板，不修改源节点或关系。

rules: 逐项核对源 description、evidence、assessmentPrompt、ageRange 和真实前后关系。
区分官方课程标准、专业框架、综合研究报告、课堂观察和小样本试点；不把课程目标写成效果证据。
记录每项来源具体支持什么，以及样本年龄、研究设计和外推限制。
外部来源核查完成不等于独立数学教研、解释内容验收或儿童理解验收。

sourceCatalog.title: WS03 — The most popular use of the play space
sourceCatalog.supports: Year 2 AC9M2ST01/02. The work sample shows a question and purpose, survey categories, data-collection method, recording/display plan, tally sheet, tally groups of five, a picture graph with one dot per student's choice, and a digital survey/display.
sourceCatalog.limitation: An official curriculum work sample and achievement illustration, not a controlled study of learning effects.

sourceCatalog.title: WS02 — Clean our school
sourceCatalog.supports: Year 3 AC9M3ST01/02/03. The standard explicitly includes categorical and discrete numerical data, frequency tables and spreadsheets; the work sample annotates participant/context identification, tabular recording, totals, picture and column graphs, interpretation and communication in context.
sourceCatalog.limitation: An official curriculum work sample, not a controlled study; its task is more extended than the narrow collection-and-recording node.

sourceCatalog.title: Pre-K–12 Guidelines for Assessment and Instruction in Statistics Education II (GAISE II)
sourceCatalog.supports: The ASA/NCTM-endorsed Level A framework connects question formulation, data collection/consideration, analysis and interpretation. It explicitly includes surveys, observations and simple experiments; categorical and quantitative variables; errors and missing values; tables, picture graphs, dotplots and bar graphs; and limiting conclusions to the group actually studied.
sourceCatalog.limitation: A professional framework, not a controlled trial. Its Levels A/B/C are developmental progressions, not fixed grade or age bands.

sourceCatalog.title: Data and Computing in K–12 Education: Foundational Competencies
sourceCatalog.supports: The elementary-school discussion distinguishes cases from attributes, recommends consistent measurement procedures, asks learners to consider who/when/where/how data were collected, and describes case-level graphs, tally marks and using displays to compare groups.
sourceCatalog.limitation: A broad consensus synthesis, not an intervention evaluating these two specific nodes.

sourceCatalog.title: Exploring Central Tendencies: The Teaching of Data and Statistics in Elementary Mathematics Classrooms
sourceCatalog.authors: Erica Litke and Heather C. Hill
sourceCatalog.supports: Analysis of 144 upper-elementary mathematics lessons found more emphasis on calculations and graph construction than on question formulation, data collection and interpretation; it also identified content-accuracy concerns. This supports keeping the whole question-to-data-to-interpretation purpose visible rather than reducing the task to making a chart.
sourceCatalog.limitation: Upper-elementary lesson observations, older than the B01 age bands; describes instructional practice and gaps, not a causal effect on student achievement.

sourceCatalog.title: Exploring Preschool Data Collection and Analysis: A Pilot Study
sourceCatalog.authors: Ashley E. Lewis Presser et al.
sourceCatalog.supports: A pilot in four preschool classrooms with 28 children used nine investigations and a teacher-facing app to scaffold question, collection, recording, graphing and data-talk steps. Pre/post scores increased from 0.58 to 0.72 (paired t(27)=5.62, p<.001), offering an example of a structured data-collection-and-analysis sequence.
sourceCatalog.limitation: Preschool sample (mean age 4.78), four classrooms, remote implementation during COVID-19, and no control group. It supports feasibility/design ideas only; it does not prove effectiveness for ages 7–9.

sourceCatalog.title: A Learning Progression for Constructing and Interpreting Data Display
sourceCatalog.authors: Eun Mi Kim, Leslie Nabors Olah and Stephanie Peters
sourceCatalog.supports: The report separates constructing data displays and interpreting data displays into two related progress variables, then designs tasks to elicit evidence for both. Its categorical-data task uses 45 survey responses, asks learners to organize and graph the same data, and then answer questions from the display.
sourceCatalog.limitation: A hypothesized progression based on literature review and expert review, not a controlled teaching intervention or direct validation for this exact age band.

sourceCatalog.title: The Role of Data Context and Task Context in Young Children's Reading of Data Representations
sourceCatalog.supports: A design-based descriptive study with 14 five-year-olds found that a familiar story context and paired pictorial/numerical table representation supported children's reading and interpretation of data.
sourceCatalog.limitation: Small descriptive study with younger children; it supports contextualized representation as a design clue, not a generalizable effect estimate for ages 7–9.

records.title: 围绕问题收集数据
records.alignment: Source description and all three evidence prompts align directly with Year 3 AC9M3ST01: acquire categorical and discrete numerical data for a question and record it with frequency tables and spreadsheets. The travel-to-school example is categorical; number of siblings is a discrete numerical count.
records.research: ACARA provides the direct Year 3 curriculum scope and a work sample showing collection, tabular recording, totals, picture/column graphs and contextual interpretation. GAISE II Level A supplies the statistical-process frame and explicitly covers surveys, observations, variable types, missing/error handling and limits on conclusions. The National Academies report adds case/attribute and data-provenance reasoning. Litke & Hill show why question formulation and collection must not be omitted in favour of graph construction alone. Presser et al. offer a structured, age-adjacent DCA sequence, but their preschool pilot cannot establish effectiveness for this age range.
coverageAudit: Define the question, target group and time/context before collecting; for travel, clarify whether the question is about the usual main travel mode or travel today.
Distinguish categorical responses (walk, car, bus) from discrete numerical values (0, 1, 2, 3 siblings).
Keep raw person-level records distinct from a frequency summary. In a frequency table, the first column is a category or numerical value and the second is its count.
Treat zero siblings as a valid value; a missing or declined response is not zero. Count each valid response once and check that frequency totals equal the number of valid responses.
Make spreadsheet entries match the source records and the frequency table; do not treat spreadsheet use as the mathematical goal itself.
designImplications: Use categories that are clear, mutually exclusive and sufficiently complete; include an 'other' option where appropriate.
For the school-travel question, specify the group and time window. Avoid collecting names, addresses or detailed routes; aggregate responses.
For sibling counts, list the actual count values and tally how many learners gave each value. Record nonresponses separately rather than folding them into zero.
Ask the learner to explain where the data came from, how each response was recorded, and why the chosen table/spreadsheet structure answers the question.
knownRisks: An ambiguous question produces answers that cannot be compared.
Overlapping or incomplete categories cause double counting or forced answers.
Confusing a raw record table with a frequency table hides what each row represents.
Treating missing responses as zero changes the data.
A class result must not be generalized to the whole school without an appropriate sampling basis.
acceptanceEvidence: The learner can state the question and who/what the data describe.
The learner can distinguish a category from a countable numerical value in the examples.
Each valid response is recorded once; tally marks, frequencies and totals agree.
The spreadsheet faithfully reproduces the data and can answer the original question.
In a changed context, the learner can choose a suitable collection/recording method and identify missing or duplicate records.
records.relationshipBoundary: Preserve the existing hard prerequisite mt_c29FaCTNsx (frequency tables build on tally charts), soft prerequisite mt_X53txVXOcG (spreadsheet recording builds on early digital data tools), and hard successors mt_kxeuXm6EyC and mt_yrvYKSwSRZ. No new dependency is inferred.

records.title: 比较两幅统计图
records.alignment: Source description and evidence align with Year 2 AC9M2ST02: create different graphical representations and compare common/distinctive features in response to questions. ACARA's Year 2 work sample specifically uses a tally sheet and a picture graph for the same survey.
records.research: ACARA's Year 2 work sample directly demonstrates survey categories, tally recording and a picture graph where one dot represents one response. GAISE II shows how the same categorical data can move from raw responses to a frequency table, picture graph and bar graph. Kim et al. distinguish constructing a display from interpreting it and provide tasks that test both. Kinnear's small study supports using familiar context alongside numerical and pictorial data representations.
coverageAudit: Both displays must encode exactly the same survey, categories, frequencies and total number of responses.
The child must answer the same concrete question from both displays, including the exact count for dogs, not only identify the most popular category.
The child must identify what remains invariant and what changes between a tally chart and a picture graph (marks/symbols, layout and any key).
The task asks which display is quicker for this question in this particular example; it must not imply that one representation is always superior.
designImplications: The current Chinese title '比较两幅统计图' is narrower than the source's English 'Comparing two data displays': a tally chart is a table, not a graph. Recommended display title: '比较两种数据表示'. This is a naming finding only; the title is not changed in this research-only batch.
For the first child-facing example, use one picture symbol for one response or make the key unmistakable; avoid adding a scale-conversion challenge that is not in the source target.
Ask: which display helps you spot the most popular pet quickly, and what feature helps? Accept a reason tied to the actual layout and question rather than a memorized rule.
Ask the same exact-count question from both displays and check that the answers match.
knownRisks: Calling a tally chart a graph blurs the difference between a table and a graphical display.
If the picture-graph key is missing or ambiguous, the count cannot be read reliably.
If one display omits a category or changes a count, the two no longer represent the same data.
Saying 'picture graphs are always easier' or 'tables are always better' overgeneralizes from one layout and purpose.
acceptanceEvidence: The learner identifies the same categories, counts and total in both displays.
The learner reads the number of dog responses correctly from each display.
The learner identifies the most popular pet and points to the evidence.
The learner explains one common feature and one different feature of the two representations.
With a new small data set or a changed pictograph key, the learner can still compare the displays and justify which is easier for a stated question.
records.relationshipBoundary: Preserve the existing hard prerequisites mt_c29FaCTNsx and mt_VhBH8wrFC6, and the hard successor mt_QpJydot2Kh. No new dependency is inferred.
